content: The information provided in the transport document must align with the certificate of the country of origin of design. This section outlines the most commonly required documents for the shipment of infectious substances, which are classified as dangerous goods. These include a Dangerous Goods Transport Document (DGTD), a spill clean-up procedure, and an air waybill. Dangerous Goods Transport Document (DGTD) As per the UN model regulations, a minimum set of information must be recorded for any infectious substance in the form of a DGTD. This document is mandatory for all shipments of Category A infectious substances (UN 2814, UN 2900) and for medical or clinical wastes (UN 3291). However, Category B infectious substances assigned to UN 3373, when packaged according to P650, are exempt from these requirements, meaning a DGTD is not required. The DGTD can take any form as long as it meets the minimum information requirements outlined in the UN model regulations and ICAO technical instructions. However, specific modal agreements or national regulations may require their own formats, such as the commonly used Dangerous Goods Declaration (DGD) form for air transport. Equivalent variations may be required for road, sea, or rail shipments as per the relevant modal agreements. The minimum information required for a DGTD includes: The sender and receiver details. The date of preparation or issuance of the document. A description of the dangerous goods. The type and net quantity of dangerous goods for each package. Handling requirements. Emergency response information. Certification (shipper’s declaration). Sender and Receiver Information The name and address of both the shipper (consignor) and the receiver (consignee) must be included. For infectious substances, the name and contact phone number of a responsible person knowledgeable about the infectious substance must also be provided. This individual should be available for contact at all times during the shipment process. Date The transport document must display the date it was prepared or provided to the initial carrier. Description of Dangerous Goods The description of the dangerous goods must include: 1. The UN number (e.g., UN 2814, UN 2900). 2. The proper shipping name (e.g., Infectious substance, affecting humans). For Category A substances, the technical name must follow the proper shipping name in brackets. 3. The hazard class or division. 4. The packing group (if applicable). 5. Any additional descriptive information required under other applicable regulations. Each dangerous good present in the package must be described. For example, if a coolant like dry ice is included, it must be listed separately with its UN number, proper shipping name, and net quantity. Handling Requirements Handling requirements specify any actions required by the carrier during the treatment of the package (e.g., loading, stowing, unloading). If no special handling is required, a statement such as No such requirements are necessary should be provided. Restrictions on the mode of transportation or routing instructions, as well as emergency arrangements, must also be included. Emergency Response Information For Category A infectious substances, the name and telephone number of a responsible person must be marked on the package and the shipper’s declaration. For Category B substances (UN 3373), the name, address, and telephone number of a responsible person must be marked on either the package or the air waybill. Emergency response information should include details such as prophylaxis for exposed individuals or spill clean-up procedures. Certification (Shipper’s Declaration) The shipper must provide a signed and dated statement on the form, acknowledging that the package has been prepared in accordance with applicable regulations. Spill Clean-Up Procedure In the event of a breach in packaging, emergency response personnel must have access to spill clean-up procedures. The following steps are recommended for cleaning up spills of infectious substances, including blood: 1. Wear gloves and protective clothing, including face and eye protection if necessary. 2. Cover the spill with a cloth or paper towels to contain it. 3. Pour an appropriate disinfectant over the cloth or paper towels and the surrounding area (e.g., 5% bleach solution or quaternary ammonium disinfectants for spills on aircraft). 4. Apply the disinfectant concentrically, starting from the outer margin of the spill area and working towards the center. 5. After 30 minutes, clear away the materials. Use a dustpan or stiff cardboard to collect broken glass or sharps and deposit them into a puncture-resistant container for disposal. 6. Clean and disinfect the spill area. Repeat steps 2–5 if necessary. 7. Dispose of contaminated materials in a leak-proof, puncture-resistant waste disposal container. 8. Report the incident to the competent authority and confirm that the site has been decontaminated. Air Waybill An air waybill is a commonly requested shipping document required for the international air transport of goods, including infectious substances. Even exempt human or animal specimens may require an air waybill, with the phrase exempt specimens included in the nature and quantity of goods box. If shipped with a coolant, the proper shipping name, UN number, and net quantity of the coolant must also be provided. The air waybill format varies across carriers, operators, and countries. It typically includes general sections outlining shipment details, such as the shipper’s and receiver’s names and addresses, carrier information, and package quantities and types. For infectious substances, the Handling information and Nature and quantity of goods sections must be carefully completed. For Category A infectious substances, a general description such as laboratory samples or infectious substance can be provided. For Category B substances, the UN number, proper shipping name, and number of packages must be included. If shipped with dry ice, the UN number, proper shipping name, and net quantity of dry ice must also be provided. Special Provisions Special provisions refer to specific circumstances or procedures not covered in standard regulations. These provisions supplement or modify the original regulations to ensure the appropriate shipment of dangerous goods. Examples include: Aqueous solutions with less than 24% alcohol by volume are not subject to these regulations. Genetically modified microorganisms (GMMOs) and organisms (GMOs) packed and marked according to specific instructions are exempt from other requirements. Decontaminated wastes that previously contained infectious substances may be considered non-regulated unless they meet the criteria of another class or division. Air transport-specific provisions include exemptions for packaging tests, quantity limits for body parts or whole bodies, and requirements for dry ice used as a refrigerant.
